subject: science
name: Reproduction: How Life Continues
summary: Living things reproduce so that their species continues. Asexual reproduction (vegetative propagation, budding, spores, fission, fragmentation) makes identical offspring from one parent; sexual reproduction joins two gametes made by meiosis, creating variation. The chapter covers flowers, pollination and seed formation, fertilisation in animals, the human reproductive systems, pregnancy, the menstrual cycle, sex determination and reproductive health.

topics.title: Why reproduce? Asexual reproduction
topics.summary: Reproduction keeps a species going. In asexual reproduction a single parent produces offspring that are copies of itself — by budding, spore formation, binary fission or fragmentation.
topics.simple: No living thing lives forever, so every species must make new individuals to survive — that is **reproduction**. In **asexual reproduction** only one parent is needed, and the babies are copies of the parent. Yeast and Hydra grow buds, bread mould makes spores, Amoeba splits in two, and Spirogyra breaks into pieces that each grow again.
topics.explain:
**Why reproduce?** Individual organisms age and die. Reproduction makes new individuals so that the **species continues** over generations. It is the only life process not needed for an individual's own survival, but it is essential for the species.

**Asexual reproduction** needs **only one parent** and **no gametes**. The offspring are genetically almost identical to the parent (they are *clones*). It is quick and can produce many offspring when conditions are good.

Main methods:
- **Budding:** a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent, grows, and then separates or stays attached. Examples: **yeast** (a unicellular fungus) and **Hydra** (a tiny freshwater animal, where the bud grows tentacles and then detaches).
- **Spore formation:** the organism makes huge numbers of tiny **spores** inside rounded structures called **sporangia**. Spores have a protective coat, are light enough to be carried by air, and grow into new individuals when they land on a moist, food-rich surface. Example: **Rhizopus**, the black bread mould.
- **Binary fission:** a single-celled organism divides into **two equal daughter cells**. The nucleus divides first, then the cytoplasm. Example: **Amoeba** (bacteria and *Paramecium* also do this).
- **Fragmentation:** the body breaks into pieces (fragments), and each fragment grows into a complete new organism. Example: the green alga **Spirogyra**.

Vegetative propagation in plants is also a kind of asexual reproduction (next topic).
topics.deep: Because asexually produced offspring are nearly identical, a whole population may be wiped out by a single disease or a sudden change in the environment. Sexual reproduction, which creates variation, reduces this risk. Many organisms (e.g. yeast, many plants) can reproduce both ways depending on conditions.
topics.example: Leave a piece of moist bread in a warm place for a few days. Fuzzy black-grey growth appears — this is Rhizopus. The tiny black dots are sporangia full of spores, which were floating in the air and landed on the bread.
keyPoints: Reproduction keeps the species going, not the individual
Asexual: one parent, no gametes, offspring are clones
Budding: yeast, Hydra
Spore formation: Rhizopus (bread mould), spores in sporangia
Binary fission: Amoeba splits into two
Fragmentation: Spirogyra breaks into pieces that each regrow

topics.title: Vegetative propagation: natural and artificial
topics.summary: New plants can grow from roots, stems or leaves instead of seeds — naturally (potato tubers, ginger rhizome, Bryophyllum leaf buds) or artificially (cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture).
topics.simple: Some plants can grow new plants from a piece of stem, root or leaf — no seeds needed. A potato's 'eyes' sprout into new plants, and a Bryophyllum leaf grows tiny plantlets along its edge. Farmers and gardeners also do this on purpose by planting cuttings, bending branches into soil, joining two plants together, or growing plants from a few cells in a lab.
topics.explain:
**Vegetative propagation** is asexual reproduction in plants using a **vegetative part** — root, stem or leaf — instead of seeds. The new plants are identical to the parent.

**Natural methods:**
- **Stem tubers — potato:** the potato is a swollen underground stem. Its 'eyes' are buds that sprout into new plants.
- **Rhizome — ginger:** an underground stem growing sideways, with buds that give rise to new shoots (turmeric also does this).
- **Leaf buds — Bryophyllum:** buds in the notches along the leaf margin grow into small plantlets when the leaf touches moist soil.

**Artificial methods (used by humans):**
- **Cutting:** a piece of stem with buds is planted in moist soil and grows roots. Examples: rose, sugarcane, money plant.
- **Layering:** a low branch is bent down and covered with soil while still attached to the parent. Once it roots, it is cut off. Example: jasmine.
- **Grafting:** a shoot (the **scion**) of a desired plant is joined onto a rooted plant (the **stock**) so they grow as one. Common for mango, apple and citrus.
- **Tissue culture:** a few cells or a tiny piece of tissue are grown on a nutrient medium in sterile lab conditions to form many identical plantlets. Widely used for **banana**, and also for orchids and other ornamental plants.

**Advantages:** faster than growing from seed; all plants keep the parent's good qualities; useful for plants that make few or no viable seeds (e.g. banana, seedless grapes). **Disadvantage:** no variation, so diseases can spread through a whole crop.
topics.example: Mango growers graft a shoot from a tree that gives sweet Alphonso mangoes onto a hardy local rootstock. The grafted tree gives Alphonso fruit and starts fruiting sooner than a tree grown from a seed.
keyPoints: Vegetative propagation = new plants from root, stem or leaf
Natural: potato (stem tuber 'eyes'), ginger (rhizome), Bryophyllum (leaf-margin buds)
Artificial: cutting (rose, sugarcane), layering (jasmine), grafting (mango)
Grafting: scion joined onto stock
Tissue culture: many identical, disease-free plantlets, e.g. banana
Offspring are identical to the parent — no variation

topics.title: Sexual reproduction, flowers and pollination
topics.summary: Sexual reproduction joins two gametes made by meiosis, creating variation. In flowering plants the flower is the reproductive organ: stamens make pollen and the pistil holds ovules. Pollination carries pollen to the stigma — by insects, birds, wind or water.
topics.simple: In **sexual reproduction**, two special cells called **gametes** (one male, one female) join together. Because the baby gets a mix from two parents, it is a little different from both — this is **variation**. In plants, the **flower** is where this happens: the **stamen** makes pollen (male) and the **pistil** has ovules (female). **Pollination** is getting the pollen onto the stigma, helped by bees, birds, wind or water.
topics.explain:
**Sexual reproduction** involves the fusion of a **male gamete** and a **female gamete**. It usually involves two parents, and the offspring get a **new combination** of features — **variation** — which helps species survive changing conditions.

**Chromosomes and meiosis:** human body cells have **23 pairs (46) chromosomes**. Gametes are made by **meiosis**, so each gamete has **half** the number (23). When two gametes fuse, the full number (46) is restored — so the chromosome number stays constant from generation to generation.

**Parts of a flower** (from outside in):
- **Sepals:** green, leaf-like; protect the bud
- **Petals:** often colourful and scented; attract pollinators
- **Stamen** (male part): **anther** (makes pollen grains) on a stalk called the **filament**
- **Pistil / carpel** (female part): **stigma** (sticky tip that receives pollen), **style** (tube-like stalk) and **ovary** (swollen base containing **ovules**; each ovule has an egg cell)

A flower with both stamens and pistil is **bisexual** (e.g. hibiscus, mustard); one with only one of them is **unisexual** (e.g. papaya, cucumber flowers).

**Pollination** = transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma.
- **Self-pollination:** to the stigma of the same flower, or another flower on the same plant
- **Cross-pollination:** to a flower on a **different plant** of the same species — gives more variation

**Agents of pollination:**
- **Biotic (living):** insects such as bees and butterflies, and birds such as sunbirds — these flowers are usually bright, scented and have nectar
- **Abiotic (non-living):** **wind** — maize, wheat, rice and grasses (small, dull flowers with lots of light, dry pollen and feathery stigmas); **water** — *Vallisneria* and some other water plants
topics.example: A bee visits a mustard flower for nectar. Pollen sticks to its hairy body, and when it lands on the next flower some rubs off onto the sticky stigma — cross-pollination done.
keyPoints: Sexual reproduction = fusion of male and female gametes → variation
Humans: 23 pairs (46) chromosomes; gametes have 23 (meiosis)
Stamen = anther + filament (male); pistil = stigma + style + ovary (female)
Ovary contains ovules; ovules contain the egg
Self-pollination (same flower/plant) vs cross-pollination (different plant)
Wind: maize, wheat, grasses; water: Vallisneria; insects and birds: bright, scented flowers

topics.title: Fertilisation in plants and animals
topics.summary: In plants, a pollen tube carries the male gamete to the ovule; fertilisation forms a zygote → embryo, the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit. Animals show external fertilisation (fish, frogs) or internal fertilisation (reptiles, birds, mammals).
topics.simple: **Fertilisation** is when a male gamete and a female gamete fuse to make one cell called a **zygote**, which grows into an **embryo**. In plants, after pollination the **ovule becomes the seed** and the **ovary becomes the fruit**. Fish and frogs release eggs and sperm into water, so fertilisation happens outside the body. In reptiles, birds and mammals, it happens inside the female's body.
topics.explain:
**Fertilisation in flowering plants:**
1. A pollen grain lands on the stigma.
2. It grows a **pollen tube** down through the style to reach an ovule inside the ovary.
3. The male gamete travels down the tube and **fuses with the egg** in the ovule.
4. This forms a **zygote**, which divides to form an **embryo**.

After fertilisation:
- **Ovule → seed** (containing the embryo and stored food, with a protective seed coat)
- **Ovary → fruit** (protects the seeds and helps them spread)
- Sepals, petals, stamens, style and stigma usually wither and fall off

When conditions are right, the seed **germinates** and the embryo grows into a new plant.

**Fertilisation in animals:**
- **External fertilisation:** eggs and sperm are released into the **water** and fuse outside the female's body. Examples: most **fish** and **frogs**. Huge numbers of eggs are released because many are eaten or never fertilised.
- **Internal fertilisation:** sperm meet the egg **inside the female's body**. Examples: **reptiles, birds and mammals** (including humans). Fewer eggs are produced, but each has a better chance of survival.

Animals whose young develop inside the mother and are born alive (most mammals) are **viviparous**; animals that lay eggs (birds, most reptiles, frogs, most fish) are **oviparous**.
topics.example: A pea pod is a fruit that grew from the ovary of the pea flower, and each pea inside is a seed that grew from an ovule. A mango is also a fruit; its big stone contains the seed.
keyPoints: Pollen tube carries the male gamete to the ovule
Male gamete + egg → zygote → embryo
Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit
External fertilisation: fish, frogs (in water, many eggs)
Internal fertilisation: reptiles, birds, mammals
Viviparous = give birth to young; oviparous = lay eggs

topics.title: Puberty and the human reproductive systems
topics.summary: At puberty the reproductive organs mature and the body changes. Testes make sperm and testosterone; ovaries release eggs and make oestrogen and progesterone. The fallopian tube is where fertilisation takes place.
topics.simple: **Puberty** is when a child's body starts turning into an adult body, usually between about 10 and 16 years. Hormones cause growth spurts, new hair, and other changes. In males, the **testes** make **sperm**. In females, the **ovaries** release one **egg** roughly every month. A sperm and an egg can meet in the **fallopian tube**, and a baby grows in the **uterus**.
topics.explain:
**Puberty** is the stage when the reproductive organs become mature. It starts at different ages for different people — often earlier in girls than in boys. Changes are caused by hormones:
- Both: growth spurt, hair in the armpits and pubic region, more active sweat and oil glands (pimples/acne are common), emotional changes
- Boys: voice deepens (the voice box grows and forms the 'Adam's apple'), facial hair, broader shoulders
- Girls: breasts develop, hips widen, **menstruation** begins

All these changes are natural, and the timing differs from person to person.

**Male reproductive system:**
- **Testes** (a pair, in a pouch called the scrotum outside the abdomen, where it is slightly cooler — needed for sperm production): make **sperm** and the hormone **testosterone**
- **Vas deferens:** tube that carries sperm from the testes
- **Seminal vesicles and prostate gland:** add fluid that nourishes the sperm and helps them move; sperm + fluid = semen
- **Urethra:** common tube for urine and semen, running through the penis

**Female reproductive system:**
- **Ovaries** (a pair): after puberty, usually **one egg is released each month**; they also make the hormones **oestrogen** and **progesterone**
- **Fallopian tubes (oviducts):** carry the egg from the ovary to the uterus; **fertilisation takes place here**
- **Uterus (womb):** a muscular, pear-shaped organ where the baby develops
- **Cervix:** the narrow lower end of the uterus
- **Vagina:** the passage from the cervix to the outside; also the birth canal

**Sperm vs egg:** a sperm is tiny, has a head (with the nucleus), a middle piece and a **tail** for swimming, and millions are produced. The egg is much larger (one of the largest human cells, about 0.1 mm), cannot move by itself, stores some food, and usually only one is released per cycle. Each carries **23 chromosomes**.
topics.example: Two classmates of the same age may look very different — one is much taller, the other has not had a growth spurt yet. This is normal: puberty begins and ends at different ages for different people.
keyPoints: Puberty: reproductive organs mature; hormones cause body changes
Testes: sperm + testosterone; kept slightly cooler in the scrotum
Sperm path: testes → vas deferens → urethra; seminal vesicles and prostate add fluid
Ovaries: one egg per month + oestrogen and progesterone
Fertilisation happens in the fallopian tube; baby develops in the uterus
Sperm: small, tail, millions; egg: large, non-motile, usually one per cycle

topics.title: Pregnancy, IVF and the menstrual cycle
topics.summary: The zygote becomes an embryo that implants in the uterus wall; the placenta supplies food and oxygen; pregnancy lasts about 9 months in three trimesters. If no fertilisation happens, the uterus lining is shed — the menstrual cycle, about 28 days long, with ovulation around day 14.
topics.simple: After fertilisation, the zygote keeps dividing and settles into the soft wall of the uterus. A special organ called the **placenta** passes food and oxygen from the mother to the baby. A pregnancy lasts about **9 months**. If the egg is not fertilised, the thick lining of the uterus is shed each month as bleeding — this is a **period (menstruation)**, a normal and healthy body process.
topics.explain:
**From zygote to baby:**
- The **zygote** forms in the fallopian tube and starts dividing as it moves to the uterus.
- The ball of cells (embryo) **implants** in the thick, soft **wall of the uterus**.
- The **placenta** forms. Through it and the **umbilical cord**, the baby gets **food and oxygen** from the mother's blood and passes **waste and carbon dioxide** back. The two bloods do not mix directly.
- From about 8 weeks, when the main organs have started to form, the developing baby is called a **foetus**.
- Pregnancy lasts about **9 months** (about 40 weeks), divided into **three trimesters** of about 3 months each.

**Maternal health:** good nutrition (iron, folic acid, protein), regular check-ups, vaccinations and delivery in a health facility keep mother and baby safe. In India, **ASHA workers** (Accredited Social Health Activists) are trained women in villages and communities who guide pregnant women, help them reach health centres and support newborn care.

**IVF (in vitro fertilisation):** egg and sperm are joined **outside the body** in a laboratory, and the early embryo is placed in the uterus. It helps couples who cannot conceive naturally. India's first IVF baby was born in Kolkata in **1978**, through the work of **Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyay** — only a few weeks after the world's first IVF baby.

**Menstrual cycle** (average about **28 days**; anything from about **21 to 35 days** is normal, and cycles can be irregular in the first years):
- **Days 1–5 (about):** **menstruation** — if no fertilisation happened, the thickened uterus lining breaks down and leaves the body as bleeding
- The lining then rebuilds and thickens
- **Around day 14:** **ovulation** — an ovary releases an egg
- If the egg is not fertilised, the lining is shed again and the next cycle begins

The first period is called **menarche**; periods stop permanently at **menopause** (usually around 45–55 years).

**Menstrual hygiene and breaking the stigma:** use clean sanitary pads, menstrual cups or clean, sun-dried cloth; change pads every 4–6 hours; wash regularly; dispose of used products properly (wrapped, not flushed). Periods are a normal biological process. There is no scientific reason to keep girls and women away from school, kitchens or any activity during menstruation, and talking about it openly helps everyone.
topics.example: Riya's periods started on 1 March and her next period started on 29 March. Her cycle length = 29 − 1 = 28 days, which is the average. Ovulation would have happened around 14 March.
keyPoints: Zygote → embryo → implants in the uterus wall
Placenta + umbilical cord: food and oxygen in, waste out
Pregnancy ≈ 9 months (≈ 40 weeks), three trimesters
ASHA workers support maternal and newborn health in India
IVF: fertilisation outside the body; India's first IVF baby 1978, Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyay
Menstrual cycle ≈ 28 days (21–35 normal); bleeding ≈ days 1–5; ovulation ≈ day 14
Menstruation is natural — hygiene matters, stigma doesn't

topics.title: Sex determination and reproductive health
topics.summary: Females are XX and males are XY; the father's sperm (X or Y) decides the baby's sex. Prenatal sex determination is illegal in India (PCPNDT Act). Reproductive health includes preventing STIs and using contraception for family planning.
topics.simple: Of our 23 pairs of chromosomes, one pair decides sex: **XX in females** and **XY in males**. The mother's egg always carries X; the father's sperm carries either X or Y — so the sperm decides whether the baby is a girl or a boy. In India it is **illegal** to test an unborn baby's sex. Reproductive health means staying safe from infections and planning a family responsibly.
topics.explain:
**Sex determination in humans:**
- 22 pairs of chromosomes are the same in males and females (**autosomes**); the 23rd pair is the **sex chromosomes**.
- **Female: XX. Male: XY.**
- Every egg carries an **X**. Half of the sperm carry **X** and half carry **Y**.
- Egg (X) + sperm (X) → **XX → girl**; egg (X) + sperm (Y) → **XY → boy**
- So the **father's sperm** decides the sex, and each pregnancy has roughly a **50:50 chance**. Blaming a mother for the baby's sex has no scientific basis.

**The law:** finding out the sex of an unborn baby for selection, and **sex-selective abortion**, are **illegal in India** under the **PCPNDT Act** (Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, 1994). This law protects girls and helps correct an unbalanced sex ratio.

**Sexually transmitted infections (STIs):** infections that spread mainly through sexual contact.
- Examples: **gonorrhoea** and **syphilis** (bacterial); **HIV–AIDS** and **HPV/genital warts** (viral)
- HIV can also spread through **infected blood**, **shared needles/syringes**, and from an infected mother to her baby. It does **not** spread by hugging, shaking hands, sharing food or mosquito bites.
- **Prevention:** correct information, using condoms, never sharing needles, using only tested blood, early testing and treatment, and vaccines where available (e.g. HPV vaccine)

**Contraception (family planning):** methods that prevent pregnancy, helping couples space births and protect the mother's health.
- **Barrier methods:** condoms (also reduce the risk of STIs), diaphragm — stop sperm from reaching the egg
- **Oral pills:** hormonal pills that stop ovulation
- **Copper-T (IUD):** a small device placed in the uterus by a doctor
- **Surgical methods** (permanent): **vasectomy** — the vas deferens is cut and tied in males; **tubectomy** — the fallopian tubes are cut and tied in females

Only condoms among these give protection against STIs.
topics.example: A couple have two daughters and some relatives blame the mother. Science shows this is wrong: the mother's eggs always carry X, and it is the father's sperm (X or Y) that decides the baby's sex — and even that is a matter of chance each time.
keyPoints: Humans: 22 pairs autosomes + 1 pair sex chromosomes
Female XX, male XY; egg always X, sperm X or Y
Father's sperm decides the sex; ~50:50 chance each time
Prenatal sex determination and sex-selective abortion are illegal (PCPNDT Act, 1994)
STIs: gonorrhoea, syphilis (bacteria); HIV, HPV (viruses)
Contraception: barrier, oral pills, Copper-T, vasectomy, tubectomy
Only condoms also protect against STIs

commonMistakes: Thinking the mother decides the baby's sex — the egg always carries X; the father's sperm (X or Y) decides.
Saying the ovary becomes the seed — the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
Mixing up pollination (pollen reaching the stigma) with fertilisation (gametes fusing inside the ovule).
Writing that fertilisation in humans happens in the uterus — it happens in the fallopian tube; the embryo then implants in the uterus.
Calling a potato a root — it is a stem tuber; its 'eyes' are buds.
Thinking gametes have 46 chromosomes — they have 23; the zygote has 46.
Believing all contraceptives protect against STIs — only barrier methods like condoms do.
Giving examples wrongly: yeast and Hydra bud, Amoeba divides by binary fission, Spirogyra fragments, Rhizopus makes spores.
revision: Reproduction keeps the species going; asexual needs one parent, sexual needs two gametes.
Budding: yeast, Hydra. Spores: Rhizopus. Binary fission: Amoeba. Fragmentation: Spirogyra.
Natural vegetative propagation: potato tuber, ginger rhizome, Bryophyllum leaf buds.
Artificial: cutting, layering, grafting (scion on stock), tissue culture (banana).
Sexual reproduction creates variation; gametes (made by meiosis) have 23 chromosomes, body cells 46.
Stamen = anther + filament; pistil = stigma + style + ovary (with ovules).
Wind pollination: maize, wheat, grasses; water: Vallisneria; insects/birds: bright, scented flowers.
After fertilisation: ovule → seed, ovary → fruit.
External fertilisation: fish, frogs; internal: reptiles, birds, mammals.
Testes → sperm + testosterone; ovaries → egg + oestrogen/progesterone; fertilisation in fallopian tube.
Placenta supplies food and oxygen; pregnancy ≈ 9 months in three trimesters.
Menstrual cycle ≈ 28 days (21–35 normal); menstruation ≈ days 1–5; ovulation ≈ day 14.

faqs.q: What is the difference between pollination and fertilisation?
faqs.a: **Pollination** is the transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. **Fertilisation** comes after it: a pollen tube grows to the ovule, and the male gamete fuses with the egg to form a zygote. Pollination can happen without fertilisation, but fertilisation in flowering plants cannot happen without pollination.

faqs.q: What is the difference between asexual and sexual reproduction?
faqs.a: **Asexual** reproduction needs one parent, no gametes, is fast, and the offspring are identical (e.g. Amoeba, yeast, potato). **Sexual** reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes, usually from two parents, and produces offspring with **variation**.

faqs.q: Who decides whether a baby is a boy or a girl?
faqs.a: The **father's sperm**. The mother's egg always carries an X chromosome. If the sperm carries X, the baby is XX (girl); if it carries Y, the baby is XY (boy). Which sperm fertilises the egg is a matter of chance.

faqs.q: Why do fish and frogs lay so many eggs?
faqs.a: They have **external fertilisation** in water. Many eggs are never fertilised, and many eggs and young are eaten or washed away. Laying huge numbers makes sure at least some survive. Animals with internal fertilisation produce fewer eggs because each has a better chance.

faqs.q: Is it normal if my periods are not exactly 28 days apart?
faqs.a: Yes. 28 days is only an average. Cycles between about **21 and 35 days** are considered normal, and in the first year or two after periods begin they are often irregular. If there are worries — very painful, very heavy or long-missing periods — it's good to talk to a parent, a school nurse or a doctor.

The placenta connects the developing baby to the wall of the uterus through the umbilical cord. It passes **food and oxygen** from the mother's blood to the baby and carries **carbon dioxide and wastes** away, without the two bloods mixing directly.

quiz.explain: Hydra (and yeast) reproduce by budding. Amoeba uses binary fission, Spirogyra fragmentation and Rhizopus spores.

quiz.q: Black bread mould (Rhizopus) reproduces mainly by:
quiz.explain: Rhizopus makes spores inside sporangia; the spores spread through air.

quiz.q: New plants grow from the buds on the leaf margins of:
quiz.explain: Bryophyllum has buds in the notches of its leaves. Potato uses stem tubers and ginger uses a rhizome.

quiz.q: Banana plants are commonly produced in large numbers by:
quiz.explain: Tissue culture produces many identical, disease-free banana plantlets from a small piece of tissue.

quiz.q: Which part of the flower receives pollen during pollination?
quiz.explain: The sticky stigma at the top of the pistil receives pollen.

quiz.q: Maize and wheat are mainly pollinated by:
quiz.explain: Maize, wheat and other grasses are wind-pollinated: they have light, dry pollen and small, dull flowers.

quiz.q: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovary develops into the:
quiz.explain: The ovary becomes the fruit; the ovules inside become seeds.

quiz.q: In which group of animals does fertilisation usually take place outside the female's body?
quiz.explain: Frogs (and most fish) release eggs and sperm into water — external fertilisation.

quiz.q: In the human female, fertilisation normally takes place in the:
quiz.explain: The sperm meets the egg in the fallopian tube (oviduct); the embryo then implants in the uterus.

quiz.q: In a 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation happens around:
quiz.explain: Ovulation (release of an egg) happens around the middle of the cycle, about day 14. Days 1–5 are menstruation.

quiz.q: India's first IVF baby was born in 1978 through the work of:
quiz.explain: Dr Subhash Mukhopadhyay achieved India's first IVF birth in Kolkata in 1978.

quiz.q: A baby receives a Y chromosome. Which statement is correct?
options: It came from the egg and the baby is a girl
It came from the egg and the baby is a boy
It came from the sperm and the baby is a girl
It came from the sperm and the baby is a boy
quiz.explain: Eggs carry only X, so a Y must come from the father's sperm; XY is male.
